description: Welcome to TURKNova! We are a dedicated team combining physics, astronomy, and engineering to turn space and climate data into impactful, science-backed solutions for Earth. Driven by analytical rigor and innovative problem-solving, we aim to build a standout project with global recognition. Please note that our team roster is currently complete and we are not accepting new members at this time.
summary:
TerraSeasons is an interactive web app that shows how fast Turkey's climate is changing in each season. Annual averages hide differences between winter, spring, summer and autumn, so we used NASA MERRA-2 monthly data (1980–2025; 2 m air temperature and bias-corrected precipitation) to measure temperature and rainfall trends per season, for Turkey and its seven geographic regions.

For every trend the app shows the rate of change per decade, a 95% confidence interval and a significance test (HAC regression, Mann-Kendall, Theil-Sen, with multiple-test correction for regions). We found that all four seasons are warming significantly, with summer fastest (about +0.57 °C per decade) and winter slowest (about +0.34 °C per decade), while seasonal rainfall trends are mostly too uncertain to separate from natural variability. Users can compare regions, periods and record seasons, and every result comes with a plain-language explanation and its limitations.

It addresses the challenge by turning NASA Earth observation data into clear, trustworthy trend information that students, planners and the public can explore.
details:
What it does: TerraSeasons shows how fast Turkey's climate is changing in each season. Using NASA MERRA-2 data (1980-2025), it measures temperature and precipitation trends per decade for winter, spring, summer and autumn, for Turkey and its seven geographic regions, with 95% confidence intervals and significance tests. Views: Overview (key findings written automatically from the data), Explore (trends, 10-year moving average, year-range slider), Regions (7 regions x 4 seasons heatmap), Compare (two areas side by side), Then vs now (1980-1999 vs 2006-2025 and seasonal stripes) and Records (warmest, coldest, wettest and driest seasons).

How it works: Monthly NASA MERRA-2 temperature (T2M) and bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) are cropped to Turkey, grid cells are assigned to regions, and cosine-latitude weighted area means are computed. Temperature is averaged by season; precipitation is summed to seasonal totals. Trends use OLS with Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, checked with Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen, and regional p-values are corrected for multiple testing (Benjamini-Hochberg, 28 tests per variable).

Main results: all four seasons warm significantly, fastest in summer (+0.57 C per decade, 95% CI +0.41 to +0.72) and slowest in winter (+0.34 C per decade, 95% CI +0.03 to +0.65). 25 of 28 regional temperature trends are significant. Rainfall is harder to confirm: only summer shows a significant national trend (+3.8 mm per decade), and 1 of 28 regional precipitation trends is significant.

Benefits and intended impact: it gives students, planners and the public a clear, explorable view of seasonal climate change in Turkey, which matters for heat and health, energy and water use, and farming. Every number is explained in plain language, so non-experts can read the results correctly.

Creativity: instead of a single annual trend, we look at the seasonal pattern, and the app writes its own interpretation text from the data, so the explanations always match the numbers. Seasonal stripes, a then-versus-now view and record seasons make the trends easy to grasp.

Factors considered: autocorrelation between years (HAC), false positives from many regional tests (BH correction), the difference between "not significant" and "no change", the coarse 55 km grid, reanalysis versus station data, a 46-year record, and that significance does not identify a cause. These limits are stated inside the app.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, matplotlib, geopandas, shapely, earthaccess; deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud; code on GitHub (github.com/denizselinozdemir/terraseasons).
